# Diagnosing Acceleration Sputtering in Legacy Fuel Systems

When a vehicle exhibits sputtering specifically during throttle application from a stop, the symptom often points to an interruption in air-fuel mixture delivery or ignition timing under load. In your specific case—a 1991 Honda Accord EX with a multi-point fuel injection system—the recent maintenance history provides critical context but likely doesn't account for all failure modes. You have replaced spark plugs, wires, distributor cap, timing belt, tensioners, and two injectors. While these components are essential for combustion efficiency, the persistence of the issue suggests looking beyond simple replacement parts toward system-level diagnostics or overlooked mechanical wear.

The feeling that the engine "wants to turn off" indicates a lean condition where the air-fuel ratio drops below the stoichiometric point required for stable combustion under load. During acceleration from a stop, the Engine Control Unit (ECU) demands immediate torque; if the fuel delivery cannot match the increased airflow through the throttle body, misfires occur. Even with new injectors installed, a clogged fuel filter remains a primary suspect. A restriction in the filter creates excessive pressure drop upstream of the injector rails, limiting flow volume exactly when the pump is working hardest to meet demand. This is a classic bottleneck scenario where component replacement fails if the supply chain isn't fully restored.

Beyond the fuel filter, consider the condition of the throttle body and intake manifold gaskets. On older Honda engines like the B-series found in your Accord, carbon buildup on the throttle plate or a sticking throttle position sensor (TPS) can cause erratic idle transitions. If the TPS sends an incorrect voltage signal to the ECU regarding pedal position, the fuel map may not adjust correctly for load. Similarly, vacuum leaks introduced by aged intake gaskets allow unmetered air into the combustion chamber. This extra air leans out the mixture, causing the engine to stumble when the throttle opens and demand more fuel than is currently being injected.

Another possibility involves the fuel pump itself or its return line. If the pump is aging, it may struggle to maintain consistent pressure during high-flow events. You can verify this by monitoring fuel pressure with a gauge while commanding wide-open throttle; if pressure drops significantly before returning to baseline, the pump or filter needs attention. Additionally, check the condition of the remaining injector you did not replace. If one injector is partially clogged and was replaced while the other remains restricted, a mismatch in spray patterns can cause uneven cylinder loading, leading to rough running conditions that mimic low fuel levels.

Finally, ensure the timing belt installation aligns perfectly with manufacturer specifications. Although you mentioned replacing it, incorrect alignment of the camshaft relative to the crankshaft will desynchronize valve opening events with piston position. This results in poor combustion efficiency under load, even if spark and fuel delivery are technically correct. Given the age of the vehicle, mechanical wear in the fuel pump or throttle linkage is just as probable as a faulty sensor. Systematic elimination of these variables, rather than assuming new parts solved everything, will isolate the root cause effectively.
